report:
**Conclusion:** The evidence on coenzyme Q10 (CoQ10) for statin-related muscle discomfort is mixed and not strong enough to confirm reliable relief. Some meta-analyses suggest a modest benefit, while a major randomized trial and another meta-analysis found no significant effect on muscle symptoms.

- A randomized trial in patients with confirmed statin myopathy found that CoQ10 raised blood CoQ10 levels but had “no observable effect on any muscle outcome.” (https://medicalresearch.com/study-finds-coenzyme-q10-no-effect-statin-myopathy/)
- A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials (Banach et al., Mayo Clinic Proceedings 2015) concluded that CoQ10 supplementation did “not suggest any significant benefit” for statin-induced myopathy. (https://jndc-chemistryarticles.info/preventive-medicine-and-care/article/effect-of-coenzyme-q-10-supplementation-on-statin-induced-myalgia-a-randomized-double-blind-placebo-controlled-study-273)
- In contrast, an updated meta-analysis (Qu et al., Journal of Clinical Pharmacology 2015) reported that CoQ10 may help prevent statin-related muscle symptoms, supporting a possible modest benefit. (https://ubiehealth.com/doctors-note/coq10-statin-muscle-ache-stop-relief-how-md-uses-751q4)
- A separate review noted that CoQ10 at 30–200 mg daily showed “beneficial effects on statin myopathy with no noted side effects,” but called for further research. (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24170646/)

Overall, CoQ10 is safe and sometimes used informally, but clinical trial results are inconsistent and it is not a guideline-recommended treatment for statin muscle pain. Patients should consult their clinician before use.
